opus-5.5.text:
I think it's overlooked because people tend to assume that once the mathematics is written down, the hard part is done, and that turning it into Lean is just a kind of translation, almost clerical work. But anyone who has actually tried to formalize a real paper knows that's not the case at all.

When mathematicians write proofs, they rely enormously on shared context. They say "it's easy to see," or "by a standard argument," or they skip steps that every expert in the subfield would fill in automatically. A human referee is fine with that. But Lean is not fine with that. Lean wants every definition pinned down, every implicit assumption made explicit, every little lemma that you'd never bother writing on a blackboard actually proved. So the gap between an informal proof and a formal one is often huge, sometimes ten or twenty times longer, and filling that gap requires real mathematical understanding, not just syntax.

There's also the infrastructure problem. Mathlib is impressive, but it covers only a slice of modern mathematics. If you want to formalize a result in, say, a niche area of algebraic geometry or analytic number theory, you often find that the basic definitions and foundational theorems you need simply don't exist yet. So before you can even state your theorem, you have to build the scaffolding underneath it. That's a massive amount of work, and it's not glamorous, so it doesn't get the attention that, you know, solving an Olympiad problem gets.

And I think that's the other reason it's overlooked: the AI for math community has been very focused on benchmarks like competition problems, where the statements are short and self-contained. That's a great testing ground, but it's not where most of mathematics lives. Real mathematics is cumulative; it's built on decades of prior results. If we want AI systems that can actually help working mathematicians, verify research, or eventually discover new things, we need that whole body of existing knowledge to be in a machine-checkable form. Autoformalization at scale is really the bottleneck for that.

So to me it's actually one of the most important problems. If you can convert existing mathematics into Lean reliably, you get a huge, verified dataset, which helps train better provers, and you get a foundation that makes new formal mathematics much easier. It's a flywheel. But you have to be willing to do the hard, unglamorous work of getting it started.

r001.rationale: It says AI math attention has focused on competition problems and that formalizing existing mathematics gets less attention than solving Olympiad problems.

r002.rationale: It describes Lean formalization as demanding and often much longer than an informal proof, but does not clearly say converting the mathematics is harder than proving it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think people underestimate it because, from the outside, it looks like translation. You have a theorem written in English and LaTeX, you have Lean, and surely a large language model can just map one onto the other. But that framing misses what formalization actually is. When a human mathematician writes a proof, they leave out an enormous amount. They say "by a standard compactness argument" or "it is easy to see that," and the reader fills in the gaps using years of shared intuition. Lean has no such intuition. Every single one of those gaps has to be made explicit, down to the level the kernel will accept. So the real work is not translating what is on the page, it is reconstructing everything that was never written down.

The second reason it is overlooked is that the hard part is often not the proof, it is the statement. Getting the definitions right is surprisingly subtle. Mathlib has its own way of defining a manifold, a measure, a group action, and those choices do not always line up cleanly with how a particular paper sets things up. If you formalize the statement slightly wrong, you can produce a perfectly valid Lean proof of something that is not actually the theorem you cared about. That failure mode is quiet and dangerous, and it is exactly where automated systems struggle most, because the model has to understand the mathematical intent, not just the syntax.

And then there is scale. The frontier of mathematics is built on centuries of accumulated results, and only a tiny fraction of that is in Mathlib today. If we want AI systems to prove genuinely new theorems in a verified way, they need the existing edifice available as formal building blocks. Right now a lot of attention goes to the exciting end, having a model discover a novel proof, and comparatively little goes to the unglamorous foundation of getting the textbooks and the research literature into a machine-checkable form. But without that foundation, the exciting results stay confined to narrow, competition-style problems. So I see autoformalization as the bottleneck for the whole field, and I think it deserves far more serious effort than it has gotten.

r001.rationale: The response says AI proof discovery gets more attention than formalizing existing mathematics and mentions “competition-style problems,” but it does not clearly identify Putnam or IMO problem solving as the comparison.

r002.rationale: The response says the hard part is often the statement rather than the proof, and explains that formalization requires reconstructing omitted details and resolving subtle definitions. This conveys that formalizing existing mathematics can be harder than proving it.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s overlooked because people often focus on what happens once a mathematical problem is already expressed in Lean: can an AI find a proof? But getting the problem into that form is itself a substantial mathematical task.

A human-written proof relies on shared context. We leave assumptions implicit, move between equivalent definitions, and say things like “it follows immediately.” Formalizing that means making those dependencies explicit and choosing representations that fit together with the existing library. A step that takes one line on paper can require a lot of work in Lean.

And there’s a distinction between verifying a formal statement and knowing that it captures the mathematics you intended. Lean can check the proof of the statement you wrote, but that doesn’t by itself establish that you translated the original claim faithfully.

So I see formalization as part of the reasoning challenge, rather than just preparation for it. If we want AI to engage with existing mathematics, it needs to bridge that gap between how mathematicians communicate ideas and what a formal system can verify.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people often focus on the more glamorous question: can AI discover a new theorem or solve a difficult problem? But even when we already know the mathematics, translating it into Lean is a substantial challenge. A human proof leaves a lot implicit. We say “clearly,” invoke a standard result, or move between equivalent definitions without explaining every step. A formal proof has to make those dependencies precise.

And it isn’t just a matter of filling in missing steps. You have to choose representations, find the right results in the library, and make sure their assumptions match what you need. Two formulations can be equivalent mathematically but very different to work with formally.

That makes formalizing existing mathematics an important test of mathematical understanding in its own right. It also builds the infrastructure for future work: the definitions, theorems, and reusable proofs that an AI system can build on. If we want AI to do mathematics that we can reliably verify, that translation layer deserves much more attention.
